newsitem.title: FRANCE: Serbia opposition to end demos if towns returned.
newsitem.headline: Serbia opposition to end demos if towns returned.

text.p: Serbian opposition leaders said on Thursday they would end weeks of protests against President Slobodan Milosevic if parliament adopted a bill on Tuesday that fully reinstated their municipal election wins in 14 cities.

The three Zajedno (Together) leaders, after talks in Paris with Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, remained cautious about the hardline Socialist president's abrupt decision to reinstate the victories after seven weeks of huge street protests.

If the bill Milosevic wants parliament to endorse on Tuesday "fully and truly" reinstates the November 17 election victories, "we will stop our demonstrations and give a chance to dialogue," Vuk Draskovic, one of the three leaders, told a news conference.

"As far as Mr Milosevic is concerned we must be very, very careful," Draskovic, speaking in English, added. "We have a very bad experience in the past. A lot of times he promised one thing and did immediately after that the other one."

The election wins, including in Belgrade, were annulled because of alleged "irregularities", prompting rallies in Belgrade by the opposition parties, students and professional groups from lawyers to actors.
If Milosevic failed to keep his promises and negotiate other democratic reforms, Draskovic added that: "It would be very easy for us to have 100,000 people on the streets of Serbia overnight".
"We think that we won just the first round for which we fought almost 90 days with great energy and feelings," said Vesna Pesic, another of the leaders at a joint news conference with de Charette.
"I don't think this is the end...we have a lot of other things to do," she said.

De Charette said Serbia's problems should be resolved by recognition of the opposition municipal wins, talks between the government and the opposition, democratic elections as planned by the end of this year and free access to the media.
"France is available to give its full support to the implementation of these (four) provisions," he said.
"I am ready to believe, I want to believe that this is the process Mr Milosevic wants to carry out, and in that case I am glad," he said.
In a policy switch, France invited Draskovic, Pesic and Zoran Djindjic, the three Zajedno leaders, to visit Paris after Serbian police used violence against peaceful demonstrators earlier this week.

France said the invitation amounted to recognition of the coalition. De Charette hailed the maturity of the coalition and, in a warm show of support, stood for the cameras shaking hands with the three leaders.
He said France would contact other EU governments to work out a common way of backing moves towards democracy in Serbia. He also said that the municipalities could count on French aid.

Draskovic said that Milosevic's decision to back-track on the election results was "good. What is not good is the fact that Mr Milosevic did this after 80 days of peaceful demonstrations all over Serbia," he said.
He added ironically that "Maybe Mr Milosevic (was not) informed about such demonstrations and maybe some few days ago someone told him about that and he acted urgently.
